title: Young people want social media redesigned and governed rather than simply removed, balancing connection and community against algorithmic pressure, AI risk, and weak trust
source_unit: UK Department for Science, Innovation and Technology, Children's wellbeing online: What young people think about social media, safety and AI, prepared by Savanta, 15 July 2026
geography: United Kingdom young people ages 10-21, parents, teachers, youth practitioners, public consultation participants, and youth-led hack events

denominator.unit: more than young people ages 10-21 completing the main online survey, with more than 5,000 parents and over 2,200 teachers/youth practitioners surveyed separately

smartphone_access.unit: percent of young people in the main survey reporting smartphone access

social_media_use.unit: percent of young people in the main survey reporting social-media use

connection_benefit.unit: percent saying social media helped them feel connected to other people

inclusion_benefit.unit: percent saying social media made them feel included

anxiety_exposure.value: 40 percent said social media sometimes made them worry about what others think, and 39 percent said it made them feel anxious; these feelings were more common among girls and disabled young people
anxiety_exposure.unit: reported survey shares and subgroup pattern

social_infrastructure.value: young people described social media as a way to reach friends, information, education, and communities that may be unavailable locally or too costly to access in person

observations.method: UK main survey of young people, parents, teachers and youth practitioners combined with seven youth-led hack events and youth collaborators.
observations.uncertainty: Survey shares describe reported experience rather than clinical wellbeing or causal effects; public-consultation respondents were self-selecting and are kept distinct from the main survey.
observations.subgroup: Young people ages 10-21, girls, disabled young people, rural youth, cultural or faith minorities, parents, teachers, youth practitioners, and youth-led communities.
observations.counterinterpretation: Connection benefits may vary by platform, household support, offline access, disability, geography, and the type of community being sought; high use does not by itself establish harm.

observations.period: 2026; blanket-ban preferences and targeted platform controls

denominator.unit: more than young people ages 10-21 in the main UK survey, with separate parent and professional surveys

young_people_full_ban.unit: percent of young people supporting a full under-16 social-media ban

young_people_selective_access.unit: percent saying under-16s should be allowed on some platforms but not others

parent_minimum_age.unit: percent of parents in the main survey agreeing social media should have a minimum age of 16

targeted_features.unit: percent of young people agreeing that restricting certain features would make social media safer, compared with 75% of parents and 82% of teachers/youth practitioners

policy_route.value: young people generally favored targeted, practical, enforceable changes over an outright ban, while parents and professionals placed more weight on strong age rules

observations.method: Main survey comparisons across young people, parents, and teachers/youth practitioners, supplemented by youth-led deliberative hack events.
observations.uncertainty: Preferences may reflect question wording, age, perceived enforceability, family rules, and local context; support for a ban or feature restrictions does not predict implementation outcomes.
observations.subgroup: Under-16s, young people ages 16-21, parents, teachers, youth practitioners, policymakers, platforms, and families with different levels of offline social access.
observations.counterinterpretation: A well-enforced age floor could reduce some exposures, while targeted controls could leave structural engagement incentives intact; the report does not adjudicate the policy tradeoff experimentally.

observations.period: 2026; platform design, algorithmic control, and institutional responsibility

denominator.unit: UK youth-led hack events across Belfast, Brighton, Caerphilly, Edinburgh, Gloucester, Ipswich, and Newcastle

design_concerns.value: young people repeatedly raised infinite scrolling, autoplay, public like counts, poor comment moderation, age-inappropriate advertising, opaque algorithms, and contact from strangers

time_limits.unit: percent of young people in the main survey supporting at least one daily-limit or overnight-access restriction

platform_responsibility.value: young people assigned platforms responsibility for moderation, algorithm design, and age verification, and government responsibility for binding standards and enforcement

incentive_awareness.value: young people linked the features they find harmful to the commercial incentives that make platforms money, reducing confidence in voluntary action

desired_route.value: the preferred response was platform-level design change and enforceable accountability rather than relying only on family willpower or individual self-control

observations.method: Seven participatory youth hack events co-designed and co-delivered with young people, plus main survey results and youth collaborators in analysis and writing.
observations.uncertainty: Hack events are qualitative and participatory rather than statistically representative; the findings show articulated concerns and proposals, not prevalence estimates for every issue.
observations.subgroup: Young people ages 10-18 participating in hack events, youth collaborators ages 16-21, platform users, parents, policymakers, and platform designers.
observations.counterinterpretation: Platform-level limits can be bypassed or create new exclusion; user control and moderation improvements also require usable defaults, appeal routes, and privacy-preserving enforcement.

observations.period: 2026; AI content, age verification, and trust

denominator.unit: main survey of young people, with separate parent/professional surveys and youth-led qualitative events

ai_concerns.value: young people identified misinformation, deepfakes, romantic or friend-like chatbots, over-reliance for schoolwork, extremist content, and AI data-centre water use as major concerns

ai_age_requirement.value: 83 percent of young people ages 16-21 and 85 percent of parents support minimum age requirements for AI chatbots; 85 percent of teachers/youth practitioners also support them

content_labeling.value: mandatory, visible labeling of AI-generated or edited content was the most consistent practical demand at the youth hack events

age_check_support.value: 66 percent of young people ages 16-21 in the main survey say age checks would help keep them safer, while youth consultation participants raised privacy, exclusion, and enforceability concerns

trust_condition.value: young people support stronger verification only when it works, is enforced, and does not create disproportionate privacy or exclusion risks

observations.method: Mixed-method UK research combining main surveys, self-selected public consultation, professional survey, youth hacks, and youth collaborators.
observations.uncertainty: AI concerns and proposals emerged strongly in qualitative events but are not all prevalence estimates; support percentages differ by age and sample frame, and the report does not evaluate a specific age-verification technology.
observations.subgroup: Young people, parents, teachers, youth practitioners, disabled and foreign-language users, platforms, schools, regulators, and AI developers.
observations.counterinterpretation: Labels, literacy, and age checks may reduce some risks but cannot alone resolve algorithmic incentives, privacy leakage, misinformation supply, or the social value of online communities.

related_sources.claim: The UK government's Growing up in the online world collection contains the full quantitative and qualitative reports and policy response.
The government's progress statement provides complementary policy context and distinguishes young people's views from a singular solution.

boundary: This record adds UK public research on young people's online connection, platform design, social-media safety, AI concerns, age verification, and youth-led policy preferences. It preserves survey, public-consultation, professional, and participatory evidence as different frames; it is not respondent-level ingestion, a clinical wellbeing study, a global youth estimate, a platform audit, or proof that a ban or feature restriction will produce the claimed outcomes.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official GOV.UK DSIT youth summary reviewed for main survey frames, connection and anxiety shares, ban and targeted-control preferences, youth hack methods, platform responsibility, AI concerns, labeling, and age-verification findings.
